# Proto-Gospel of James Chapter 18 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** P.Bodmer V / Greek MSS, Proto-Gospel of James 18 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/POX_018_page_001.jpg

---

## Chapter 18

**18:1** And he found a cave there and brought her into it, and he left his sons with her, and went out to seek a Hebrew midwife in the region of Bethlehem.

**18:2** Now I, Joseph, was walking, and I walked and yet did not walk. And I looked up to the vault of heaven and saw it standing still. And I looked at the air, and I saw the air in amazement. And I looked at the birds of heaven, and they were stationary. And I looked down at the ground, and I saw a vessel lying there and workers reclining beside it, with their hands in the vessel. And those who were chewing were not chewing. And those who were lifting were not lifting. And those who were raising something to their mouths were not raising it. And the faces of all were looking upward.

**18:3** And I saw sheep being driven, and they stood still. And the shepherd raised his hand to strike them, and his hand remained raised. And I saw a stream of water, and the mouths of the kids bowed down toward it and were not drinking. And then all at once everything resumed its course.

**18:4** And behold, a woman was coming down from the hillside, and she said to me: "Man, where are you going?" And I said: "I am seeking a Hebrew midwife." She said: "Are you from Israel?" I said: "Yes." She said: "And who is it who labors in the cave?" I said: "My betrothed." She said: "Is she not your wife?" I said: "She is Mary, who was raised in the temple of the Lord. I received her by lot as my wife, yet she is not my wife — she has conceived by the Holy Spirit."

**18:5** And the midwife said: "Is this true?" And Joseph said: "Come and see." And the midwife went with him.

---

## Translator's Note

Chapter 18 contains the most extraordinary passage in the Protevangelium and arguably one of the most audacious moments in all early Christian literature. The first-person voice of Joseph ("I, Joseph") intrudes suddenly into what has been a third-person narrative, creating a documentary immediacy. The vision of universal stillness — sky, air, birds, workers, shepherd, goat-kids, a stream — is a cosmic birth-stop, a suspension of time at the moment of the Incarnation. The literary technique (multiple iterations of the same frozen image, each slightly different) creates a cumulative, trance-like effect. This passage was enormously influential in Byzantine liturgical art and hymnody — especially the Christmas kontakion tradition. The resumption "all at once" (18:3) is a narrative return to real time as the birth occurs off-page.
